newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma says Pepsi withdrawal won't hit investments.
newsitem.headline: Burma says Pepsi withdrawal won't hit investments.

text.p: Burma said on Saturday that Pepsi's decision to stop doing business with the military-ruled country would not jeopardise future investments from other multinationals.

"That will not affect the climate of foreign investment (in Burma)," Foreign Minister Ohn Gyaw said in response to a question on the implications of Pepsi's withdrawal. He was speaking at a monthly government news conference in the Burmese capital.
PepsiCo Inc, which last year sold its 40 percent stake in a Burmese venture after growing pressure from human rights groups, said on Tuesday it would cease all ties with Burma.
The U.S. soft drinks giant said it had ended an agreement to sell syrup to its franchise bottler in Rangoon.

But Pepsi was still freely available in the capital after the announcement, Pepsi billboards were still up across Rangoon and some retailers said they had not even heard the news about Pepsi's withdrawal.
The owner of the Pepsi franchise in Burma, U Thein Tun, was not available for comment. A company official said he was away doing Buddhist religious rites.

Rights groups accuse Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), which seized power in 1988 after crushing pro-democracy protests, of being involved in human rights abuses and suppressing democracy.
The SLORC has also been at odds with opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who has urged foreign businesses not to invest in Burma until the situation improves.
Business analysts predicted that Pepsi's withdrawal could spark further pullouts by other multinationals already doing business in the county.
Among the companies that had already pulled out of Burma since last year are Liz Claiborne, Spiegel Inc unit Eddie Bauer, Heineken NV and Carlsberg.
Rights activists said they now plan to target major oil companies operating in Burma, including Unocal, Total, Atlantic Richfield Co and Texaco.
Ohn Gyaw said some other foreign businesses were defying the campaign to stop investments in Burma and had shown interest in wanting to do business with the country.
A senior official of the Myanmar Investment Commission told reporters that the investment picture had improved despite the negative publicity.
A total of $5.36 billion had been invested by foreign investors in 237 Burmese projects by the end of January this year, he said.
Latest data showed that in the first 10 months of the 1996/97 fiscal year (April-March), a total of $2.12 billion in new investments in 68 project had been received by Burma.
This was up from the $514 million in new investments in 35 projects made in the same period in the 1995/96 financial year, he added.
